New version 0.1.2 contains support for LCA001 hue saturation mode.

Hi, I solved this in my installation by using the group integration and a template sensor. I am using 20 lights.
Unfortunately you still have to setup 100 lights in the powercalc integration and define them in the group. But you only need to do this one time.

Step1 - Setup powercalc:

```yaml
sensor:
  - platform: powercalc
    entity_id: light.livingroom
  - platform: powercalc
    entity_id: light.bedroom
```

Step2 - Create a group of the power sensors created by powercalc

```yaml
group:
  all_light_power:
    name: All lights power
    entities:
      - sensor.livingroom_power
      - sensor.bedroom_power
```

Step3 - Define a template sensor summing all the power values

```yaml
sensor:
  - platform: template
    sensors:
      all_light_power:
        friendly_name: All light power
        unit_of_measurement: W
        icon_template: mdi:transmission-tower
        value_template: >
          {{ expand('group.all_light_power') 
          | rejectattr('state', 'in', ['unavailable', 'unknown'])
          | map(attribute='state') | map('float') | sum | round(2) }}
```

When you add a new light you only need to add this to the powercalc integration and the group.

> I was looking over the code and I see no reason to limit fixed mode domains at all. The logic is actually really well done and should work with most domains to be honest.
> 
> Is there a reason to limit domains with fixed mode? Do you mind if I add media_player as well?

One of the reasons I filtered domains was to limit selection of entities when you are using VS code addon.
It makes no sense to setup a power sensor for a entity not having an on/off state (for example `sensor`).
I did a quick look through possible domains and picked the ones which seem to fit to me. However I missed some, `media_player` and `remote` can be turned on and off, so they can be used for the fixed power mode.
Yes please add `media_player` also, than I will merge the changes.
Thank you very much! That was I what looking for.

With the Riemann Integral integration. Physically energy usage (kWh) is the integration of power (W) and the integral integration does exactly this. A example configuration can be seen below.

- platform: integration

I think your observations are quite normal. In order to control the brightness of an LED in a controlled manner, the change in current must be oriented exactly to the non-linear current-voltage characteristic of the light-emitting diode. The LED is a diode and initially reacts only minimally or not at all when the supply voltage increases. Only when the forward voltage is reached does the current and thus the luminous efficacy rise steeply. A dimming similar to the light bulb would therefore have to result in a completely different correlation between the input variable (position of the control potentiometer) and the output variable (light output of the LED). In modern dimmable LED power supplies, the signal of a phase angle control is converted into a control current with the help of an evaluation circuit, the level of which determines the brightness of the LED. Depending on the driver circuit, which also has losses and an inherent consumption, dimming thus does not necessarily result in linear patterns.

@marithpl I did have the same problem when creating a "energy group". The TLDR Version is that you have to create a integration sensor for each powercalc sensor so each of these integration sensors gets triggers every 10 min (or whatever you specified as an scan_interval). If you want to create light groups, then create a template sensor which sums up all integration sensors. 
I have 1 template below which helps creating all integration sensors . The template sensor creates integrations sensors for all power sensors (so not just the powercalc ones), you can paste the template in dev tools--> templates and copy the config created by the template into your configuration.yaml (or only the ones you need)

````yaml
{% for state in states -%}
{%- if state.attributes.unit_of_measurement == "W" and state.attributes.device_class == "power" -%}
- platform: integration
  source: {{ state.entity_id }}
  unit_prefix: k
  round: 2
{% endif -%}
{%- endfor -%}
````
An "energy group" sensor can then look like this:
`````yaml
- platform: template
  sensors:
    energy_server:
      friendly_name: "Alle Server Energieverbrauch"
      unit_of_measurement: kWh
      value_template: >-
        {{states('sensor.kingkong_power_kwh') | float + states('sensor.kinglouie_power_kwh')|float}}
      attribute_templates:
        last_reset: "1970-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"
        state_class: measurement
        device_class: energy
        icon: mdi:counter
``````

I dont know the cause of the problem exactly, but my suggestion is that the integration integration only updates, if the underlying sensor updates. With the new powercalc update with scan_intervals we fixed that. If we create a template sensor which sums up all powers of an specified category, the template sensors only updates its state when the values from the values template changes which it doesnt if you have a constant power like the standby-usage. So if you do it the way i specified, the integration integration gets regulary triggered by the scaninterval and will calculate the energy unregarding that the power value itself didnt change. The "energy group" sensor gets triggered when the kWh value changes from the underlying sensors which should then happen often cause this is an evergrowing and as a consequence changing value.

I suggest the following default naming convention.
Let's assume you have a light bulb with the name "Livingroom" and the entity_id is `light.livingroom`.
The component will create the following two sensors in this example:
- `sensor.livingroom_power` (name "Livingroom power")

As I mentioned in my other PR, I wrote this simple python script that reads an hs file and outputs a similar file with any desired step of brightness/hue/saturation using the interpolation provided by `scipy.interpolate` (which is computationally intensive, I would definitely not use this in real-time code):

```
import csv
import numpy as np
from scipy.interpolate import griddata
from typing import Iterator

FILENAME='export/LLC001/hs.csv'

def inclusive_range(start: int, end: int, step: int) -> Iterator[int]:
    i = start
    while i < end:
        yield i
        i += step
    yield end

def main():
    grid_bri,grid_hue,grid_sat = np.mgrid[1:256:1,1:65536:1000,1:255:1]
    points = []
    values = []

    with open(FILENAME) as csvfile:
        reader = csv.reader(csvfile, delimiter=',')
        next(reader, None)
        print("bri,hue,sat,watt")
        for row in reader:
            #print("%d,%d,%d,%.12g"%(int(row[0]),int(row[1]),int(row[2]),round(float(row[3]),2)))
            point = [row[0],int(row[1]),row[2]]
            points.append(point)
            values.append(row[3])

        fullgrid = griddata(points, values, (grid_bri,grid_hue,grid_sat), method='linear')

        for bri in inclusive_range(1, 255, 20):
            for sat in inclusive_range(1, 254, 40):
                for hue in inclusive_range(1, 65535, 2000):
                    print("%d,%d,%d,%.12g"%(bri,hue,sat,round(fullgrid[int(bri-1),int((hue-1)/1000),int(sat-1)],2)))

if __name__ == "__main__":
  main()
```

I have played around a little and I figured out a template to get all the power sensors related to an existing light group. Also modified, cleaned up and tested the power and energy sensor for light domain.
Also did rewrite the template to the new format. The old format is deprecated and should not be used anymore, so imo we must use the new format in the documentation

```yaml
light:
  - platform: group
    name: Outdoor lights
    entities:
      - light.driveway
      - light.terras

template:
  - sensor:

    # Create power sensor for a light group
    # In expand function you can set your light group id
    - name: Outdoor lights power
      unit_of_measurement: W
      icon: mdi:transmission-tower
      state: >
        {% set group_entities = expand('light.outdoor_lights') | map(attribute='attributes.entity_id') | list | first %}
        {% set ns = namespace(states=[]) %}
        {% for s in states.sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'equalto', 'power') | list %}
          {% if s.attributes.source_entity in group_entities %}
            {% set ns.states = ns.states + [ s.state | float ] %}
          {% endif %}
        {% endfor %}
        {{ ns.states | sum | round(2) }}

    # Create energy sensor for a light group
    - name: Outdoor lights energy
      unit_of_measurement: kWh
      device_class: energy
      icon: mdi:transmission-tower
      state: >
        {% set group_entities = expand('light.outdoor_lights') | map(attribute='attributes.entity_id') | list | first %}
        {% set ns = namespace(states=[]) %}
        {% for s in states.sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'equalto', 'energy') | list %}
          {% if s.attributes.source_entity in group_entities %}
            {% set ns.states = ns.states + [ s.state | float ] %}
          {% endif %}
        {% endfor %}
        {{ ns.states | sum | round(2) }}
      attributes:
        last_reset: "1970-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"
        state_class: measurement

    # Create power sensor for all powercalc sensors of light domain
    - name: All light power
      unit_of_measurement: W
      icon: mdi:transmission-tower
      state: >
        {{ states.sensor 
        | selectattr('attributes.unit_of_measurement', 'equalto', 'W') 
        | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'equalto', 'power') 
        | selectattr('attributes.source_domain', 'equalto', 'light') 
        | map(attribute='state') | map('float') | list | sum }}

    # Create energy sensor for all powercalc sensors of light domain
    - name: "All light energy"
      unit_of_measurement: kWh
      device_class: energy
      icon: mdi:transmission-tower
      state: >
        {{ states.sensor 
        | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'equalto', 'energy') 
        | selectattr('attributes.source_domain', 'equalto', 'light') 
        | map(attribute='state') | map('float') | list | sum }}
      attributes:
        last_reset: "1970-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"
        state_class: measurement
```

Hi @mariwing 
Climate entities are supported for the integration, but you are correct this is limited to devices which have a known and constant power usage. An airconditioner is not such a device and the only way to measure that power consumption is by adding a powermeter (smartplug) between the outlet and the airconditioner.

Have a look at the readme at particular the section about [calculation modes](https://github.com/bramstroker/homeassistant-powercalc#calculation-modes). For oven and floor heating you are interested in the `fixed` mode.
With this mode you can just set a power wattage for when the device is on. When you want to set a power mode per state (for example heating or cooling) you can use the `power_states` option.

Also see #95 #98 #60 for more information.

You can do the same with some template sensors, but this integration will make your life easy, as it is just a few lines of configuration. Additionaly this integration automatically creates energy sensors (kWh) to visualise consumption in the energy dashboard.

Hope this helps.

- Smartplug with energy measurement capabilities. I am using Shelly Plug S (but there are also scripts for Kasa, Tasmota and Tuya based smart plugs).

Hmm, you are correct. 
The `name` option will change both the complete name and entity_id for the power sensor. It will not postfix with `_power` of `_energy` automatically, as this `name` option allows users to modify the complete name of the power sensor.

The energy sensor however does not look at this name, but will just derive the entity_id from the source entity, in your case `device_tracker.00_25_22_19_d1_54`

So I can think of three solutions:
- Still add `energy` and `power` to the configured name automatically, but this will be a backward compatibility issue, because users which have configured `My Light Power` will get `My Light Power Power`.
- Introduce a separate option `energy_sensor_name`, which give you complete control over the energy sensor name and entity_id. But we also generate utility_meters, so that one will also give problems.
- Introduce an option `base_entity_id` which will be used to customize the generated entity id's. Let's assume your set this to `nas`, than `sensor.nas_power`, `sensor.nas_energy`, `sensor.nas_energy_daily`, `sensor.nas_energy_weekly`, `sensor.nas_energy_monthly` will be created.

I think option 3 will be the best as it will not create any breaks for users using the existing options, and it is clear what the purpose of the configuration option is.

Idea is to add a `create_group_entity` property to your first configuration.

```yaml
sensor:

    entities:
      -  entity_id: light.hallway
      -  entity_id: light.living_room
         linear:
              min_power: 0.5
              max_power: 8
```

Hi Magnus,

After switching the light to another brightness settings the script will try to get a measurement from your Fibaro FGWP102 through the HA API. It checks whether the measurement timestamp is actually more recent than when the light was changed.
This is not the case and the script stops with an exception "Power measurement is outdated. Aborting after 5 retries".

This issue arrises because of the characteristics of Zwave devices. They only communicate a new value on set intervals or when the power differs a certain amount from a previous reading. You could check the Zwave node configuration to see if the interval is set as low as possible.
You could also play around with the sleep times in `.env`, `SLEEP_TIME` and `MAX_RETRIES`. Set them both a little higher. The script will take longer to complete measurements, but maybe this helps for your case.

I am also working on a powermeter implementation which directly connects to ZwaveJS server. See #185. We maybe have discovered a way to request a new value from the zwave mode (polling), regardless of the interval setting. Will do some more work on this the next days.

Hi,

This is not what the utility-meter is meant for. This component just create several [utility-meter](https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/utility_meter/) sensors. These sensors accumulate the kWh until the cycle time (daily, hourly etc) is elapsed and then reset themself. 

For example if you have a light `light.living` powercalc creates the following sensors:
- sensor.living_power (actual estimated power in W)
- sensor.living_energy (total energy in kWh, never resets, uses `sensor.living_power` as source)
- sensor.living_energy_daily (energy usage in kWh for the day, resets at 00.00, uses `sensor.living_energy` as source)
- .. other utility-meters

You need to have a look into some template sensor to facilitate your use case, but powercalc canot help with that.

Thread #330 is not intended to show accuracy of smart-plugs - it contains only information about power draw by smart-plug itself (there are shown also models without ability of any metering).

@bramstroker ability to manual measure by providing separately measured voltage and current make no sense, because it don't use power factor (which in case of LED-bulbs is really much lower than 1), so calculated power draw will have really much overstated values. So in my opinion script with such ability should never be published (as  producing files with wrong values it will destroy our LUT database).

**I would like to emphasize it by speaking really loudly: just don't make any moves that might destroy the whole meaning of the powercalc project.**

This method of measure produces values with VA as unit of measure - so it is not suitable to use when W is really needed.
For alternating current value in VA is different than value in W for any non-resistance load (like LED-bulb, Led-driver and so on).
Quick example:
0.01A, 230V, power factor (cosinus fi) 0.6

Pa=2.3VA (apparent power measured in VA or simply calculated by multiply measured voltage and current)
but 
P=1.38W (real power measured in W, and this value should be in LUT database)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_power#Alternating_current_without_harmonics
**without dedicated power meter it is impossible to measure power factor, so using just ordinary multimeter with ability to measure alternating current isn't enough!**

Smart-plugs have small accuracy and are unsuitable to measure very low power, but they have built-in measuring system able to measure power factor and use it to show real power.

Power factor can have variable value (and it usually have), so we can't say: "use for example 0.6" because it is not true - it depends on electrical design of LED-drivers, so it depends on current brightness/model/manufacturer.
There are model which have power factor between 0.4 and 1 (depending on brightness/colour/saturation/hue) and there are models with for example power factor 0.5 in nearly all points of characteristic.

Hi, I don't understand your question fully, hope this answers your question.

Powercalc creates virtual power sensors based on a library of pre-measured lights (on all kind of brightness settings) or with custom configuration (fixed and linear mode). We also measured standby power of the lights as this really adds up when you have a lot of them.

The smart plugs you already have are real devices (and out of scope for powercalc). i.e. powercalc has no way to change the state of these entities. So when you the relevant smart plugs don't have an option to also measure their own usage I'm afraid powercalc cannot facilitate anything for that.
I also have 6 Zwave smart plugs myself and only 2 of them have an option to activate self measurement. The others also show 0 watt when they are off. You could be resolve this with a template sensor though when I think about this some more.

This is a special (and rare) case - LED1537R6 and LED1739R5 are in reality different models, and they have different characteristics. 
It can be seen even in the model numbers itself - it is in format:
LEDyynntpp
yy - design year 
nn - model number (in that year, maybe week based)
t - bulb type (G=globe, R=reflector/PAR. C=candle, T=tube - really closer to cylinder shape, etc.)
p or pp - max power draw (rounded to 0 decimals)

BDW in fact PAR (parrabolic reflector) nor reflector does not really exist in the implementation of LED (it is just taken from names of incandescent bulbs).

Koenkk's database 
https://www.zigbee2mqtt.io/supported-devices/
has some errors inside (it is just build by users), so best way is correcting this database.

As a quick and really DIRTY workaround simple model mapping should be sufficient (in `const.py` file).

This is exactly how it is working now.
Internally powercalc builds two ranges. 1-255 and minpower-maxpower.
When you only supply maxpower 40 it will set the power range to 0-40 now.
And the power will be looked up by ratio, so for 30/255 it will be 30/255s of the max power.

I have checked the code and it's working as follows. Assuming a `SLEEP_TIME` of 30 seconds.

1. Set light to a certain setting (keep track on what time this was done)
2. Wait for 30 seconds (`SLEEP_TIME`)
3. Get the power reading (from the HA API).
4. When this reading was earlier than the time in step 1, go to step 5. Else continue with a the next light setting (step 1)
5. Wait 1 second
6. Take another power reading. When this is still not recent enought, go to step 5 again, until max 5 retries.

We could improve a bit to also use the `SLEEP_TIME` setting for step 5, instead of setting this to 1.

However I doubt if this will solve your issue to get the script working with the Zwave plug robust enough.

It seems the Zwave plug is not reporting frequent enough to HA (you could check this at developer tools, go to "set state", select your entity and note the last changed date).

I have made a [PR](https://github.com/home-assistant/core/pull/57437) some time ago in home assistant core. With this development I should be able to call `refresh_values` to force the Zwave node to communicate a new power meter reading. However this PR is not merged and I doubt it will ever happen. So there is not much I can do about it now.

Zwave devices don't communicate that often as to not overload the Zwave network. Zwave has a very small bandwidth, so one node reporting every second or few seconds, will quickly make your network unresponsive and cause timeouts.

Also tested with similar configuration as in your example

```yaml
- platform: powercalc
  entity_id: light.vitrinekast
  standby_power: 0.05
  multiply_factor: 3
  multiply_factor_standby: false
  linear:
    max_power: 100
```

Powercalc will set 0.05 as the corresponding power for brightness 0 (which reflects the light off state).
When you don't specify a standby_power than 0 watt will be used for brightness 0.

The max_power is set to brightness 255 (when the light is at full brightness). In this case 100.

Powercalc calibrates the light at (0=0.05W, 255=100W)

This results in the following power readings:

```
0: 0.05
1: 1.32
2: 2.49
3: 3.69
4: 4.86
...
255: 300
```

The formula will be the following (simplified at littlebit).

power = ((max_power - min_power) * (bri / max_brightness) + min_power) * multiply_factor

So for brightness 1:
`((100 - 0.05) * (1 / 255) + 0.05) * 3` = `(99.95 * 0.00392 + 0.05) * 3` = 1.32

When you don't configure a standby power than the power on brightness 1 will be 1.17

This is really strange, because nothing related to scan_interval / update_frequency have been changed. It should alway be spikey because powercalc/HA only record a new state value every 10 minutes by default.

I have a better way for your use case anyway, but I will explain that later.

Let me first explain how the current method you use works.
- Powercalc creates both a power and energy sensor. The energy sensor is just a riemann integral sensor https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/integration/, which integrates the power sensor to kWh over time.
- The power sensor will always show 215 and this will also be the current state of the power sensor
- For the riemann integral sensor to calculate the kWh a state change for the power sensor needs to be published to HA. Normally no state change is published when the power sensor stays the same, but powercalc forces that based on the `scan_interval` which you can configure on the global configuration. This is 10 minutes by default (I would not suggest to set this much shorter, as this will cause many state changes and make your DB grow large quickly.

You can zoom your graph a bit to see if previously Before 19 feb 21:00 the energy sensor increment each 10 minutes (which it should).
I have no clue as to why the energy sensor is only updating each few hours now. Did you only upgrade powercalc or did you also upgrade HA itself?

Now the alternative (better) approach for your use case. Have a look at https://github.com/bramstroker/homeassistant-powercalc#daily-fixed-energy. 
Which allows you to do this:

```yaml
- platform: powercalc
  name: Average Standby Power energy
  daily_fixed_energy:
    value: 215
    unit_of_measurement: W
    update_frequency: 600
```

The default upgrade frequency is 30 minutes. I have set it to 600 seconds now, but you can set that even shorter if you want. However the statistics for the energy dashboard are only calculated once an hour, so setting it shorter does not really make any sense.

> I looked up RMS Current and found this formula:
Current = RMS Current x sqrt(2)
= 1.57 x 1.41
= 2.2A

Formula above works only for resistive load, but for LED bulbs and lights it is NOT resistive load at all.

> Basically the plug itself is working out the correct wattage using (I'm assuming) the voltage and current readings. I've no idea how they get 21W from the 1570 and 238 measurements

Power isn't calculated from (exposed) voltage and current readings, it is calculated inside measuring system and it is also exposed, so even exposed current value is improper it does not matter (it is different data output from measuring system, processed properly or NOT by smartplug firmware).
I think: reported current value can be peak current value (not RMS) so it is useless, but more likely this value is completely wrong.

Simple explanation why power value in W isn't just I*U (for alternating current WITHOUT harmonics)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_power#Alternating_current_without_harmonics
but for energy receiver like LED bulb it is really more complicated (because they have impulse power supply build-in so power draw is nonlinear)


> We see that the state is registering as 0W which is not true. I just assume its rounding down. 

For low values it is just filtered out (it is NOT rounding down, it is cut off, due to noise signal, it done this way just to be sure that exposed power value won't be negative :P), just it is technical limitation of measuring system used inside all smart plugs I've ever seen.

> If someone can explain the formula it means I can run the measure tests on a single bulb/device.

It is just impossible - power draw of single bulb in low brightness state (and in standby) is lower than interfering noise signal measured by smart plug.

However you can just use this LUT in your HA installation.
You have two options for this.
1. Add to `config/powercalc-custom-models` directory. powercalc will look into this directory when it cannot find the LUT in `config/custom_components/powercalc/data` directory. Then set the correct manufacturer and model (corresponding to the directory names) in your sensor configuration.
2. Use the `custom_model_directory` option. Here you directly refer to a LUT directory.

For example:
```yaml
  - platform: powercalc
     entity_id: light.lightstrip_tv
     custom_model_directory: config/powercalc-custom-models/_devices/lightstrip_tv
```

This is by design. The `include` option only includes entities which can be auto configured.

It is also in the readme.

```
Note: only entities will be included which are in the supported models list (these can be auto configured). You can combine include and entities to extend the group with custom configured entities.
```

When you want to add a manual configured entity to the group you can just do as follows:

```yaml
- platform: powercalc
   create_group: Lichten woonkamer
   entities:
     - entity_id: light.ledstrip_vooraan_level_on_off
        linear:
          calibrate:
            - 1 -> 0.1
            - 10 -> 0.3
            - 50 -> 2.3
            - 100 -> 5.7
            - 166 -> 12.2
            - 199 -> 18.3
            - 231 -> 27.2
            - 255 -> 36.5
   include:
     area: Woonkamer
```

Which will add manually configured `light.ledstrip_vooraan_level_on_off` to the group PLUS the automatically configured lights from area Woonkamer.

Thanks, reproduced it with the same setup and it is fixed now.

**Cause:** `_select_new_sub_profile()` reloaded the standby power straight from the power profile:

```python
self._standby_power, self._standby_power_on = _get_standby_power_from_profile(self.hass, self._power_profile)
```

That is the profile-only path, so it discarded anything configured on the sensor. Your `standby_power_on: 0.5` therefore survived setup and was replaced by the profile value (0 W for the sub profiles that do not declare it) on the first day to night switch.

**Fix:** resolve through the sensor config as well, so a switch applies the same precedence as setup - sensor config first, power profile second:

```python
self._standby_power, self._standby_power_on = _get_standby_power(
    self.hass,
    self._sensor_config,
    self._power_profile,
)
```

`standby_power` (the OFF state value) is resolved by the same call, so a configured `standby_power` is now also kept across switches instead of falling back to the profile.

**Regression test:** `test_reolink_keeps_configured_standby_power_on_on_sub_profile_switch` in `tests/power_profile/device_types/test_camera.py`, using the existing `reolink_camera` profile (day `2.51 W`, night `4.08 W`) with `standby_power_on: 0.5`:

- day state: `2.51 + 0.5 = 3.01 W`
- after the automatic switch to `night`: `4.08 + 0.5 = 4.58 W`

Without the fix the second assertion reads `4.08 W`, so the test fails exactly on the value you reported being dropped.
